cards.title: Polynomial-time cost sharing with concave edge costs
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, for every n-series-parallel connection game with nonnegative, nondecreasing, discrete-concave shareable edge costs and fixed player-specific delays, and every supplied path profile P, runs in time polynomial in the input bit length and outputs a path profile Q and a polynomial-time evaluable separable cost-sharing protocol ξ such that C(Q)≤C(P) and Q is a pure Nash equilibrium under ξ? The game, encoding, cost and equilibrium are defined below. This asks for the polynomial-time extension of the source’s fixed-cost reduction to its stated concave-cost class; it does not require a prescribed sequence of steps from the original algorithm.
cards.why: Tests whether economies of scale can be combined with efficiently computed, exactly stable local cost allocations on a graph class that already supports the required existence theorem. A polynomial reduction would transfer algorithmic welfare guarantees to strategic network formation.
cards.status_note: Recovered the graph, user-count cost and private-delay restrictions from the primary conference text and full arXiv version. Both state the concave running-time question. Checked the 2020/2021 journal metadata and abstract and searched subsequent work and the authors’ publication lists; no resolution matching this extension was found. Journal full text was inaccessible, so this is a source-grounded open question with a limited later-version check, not a proof that no later solution exists.

progress.text: Theorem 10 proves an efficient fixed-cost reduction on n-series-parallel networks with player-specific delays. Its following remark leaves the concave-cost running-time guarantee open.
Journal version published online; the publisher’s fixed-cost abstract and bibliographic metadata were checked, without access to its full text.

sentences: Players choose terminal-connecting paths and split the edge costs while paying their own fixed delays.
On the source’s n-series-parallel networks, a low-cost allocation can be transformed into an equilibrium without increasing social cost.
For fixed edge costs this transformation is polynomial-time; for concave costs the source leaves its running time open.
The card asks for a polynomial-time transformation with exact budget balance and an efficiently evaluable local sharing rule.
The full 2018 source was checked; the later journal abstract was accessible, but its full text was not.

cards.definitions: There are n≥1 unweighted players and a finite undirected loopless multigraph G=(V,E), with parallel edges distinguished. Each player i has distinct connected terminals sᵢ,tᵢ and may choose any simple sᵢ–tᵢ path. The graph is irredundant: every vertex and edge lies on a permitted path of at least one player. For each i, let Gᵢ be the union of all its permitted paths. The n-series-parallel promise means Gᵢ can be obtained from a single edge with terminals sᵢ,tᵢ by repeatedly subdividing an edge into two edges through a new vertex, or adding an edge parallel to an existing edge, preserving the two terminals. This promise concerns each player’s path subgraph; treewidth at most two for G alone is insufficient. For each edge e the input lists rational values cₑ(0),…,cₑ(n), with cₑ(0)=0 and increments cₑ(j)−cₑ(j−1) nonnegative and nonincreasing for j=1,…,n. The total shareable cost depends only on the number of users, not their identities or weights. The input also gives a nonnegative rational delay dᵢ,ₑ for each player and edge. Graph data, terminals and a supplied simple path Pᵢ for every player are explicit; rational numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary. This finite-table convention makes the source’s polynomial-time question precise; it imposes no bound on the magnitudes of the costs. For a profile R, set Nₑ(R)={i:e∈Rᵢ} and C(R)=∑ₑcₑ(|Nₑ(R)|)+∑ᵢ∑ₑ∈Rᵢdᵢ,ₑ. A protocol gives nonnegative rational shares ξᵢ,ₑ(S) for user sets S⊆{1,…,n}. Shares are zero for i∉S and sum over i∈S to cₑ(|S|). A share depends on the edge and its user set; it may also use the fixed game data and the computed output, but cannot depend on choices made on other edges. Player i’s private cost at R is πᵢ(R)=∑ₑ∈Rᵢ(ξᵢ,ₑ(Nₑ(R))+dᵢ,ₑ). A pure Nash equilibrium Q satisfies πᵢ(Q)≤πᵢ(Q₋ᵢ,Rᵢ) for every i and every permitted alternate path Rᵢ. The protocol must be stable for this game, meaning some pure equilibrium exists; the returned Q witnesses this. The algorithm returns polynomially many bits describing ξ, with a fixed deterministic evaluator that, given the game, this description, i,e and the n-bit indicator of S, returns the exact share in polynomial time. It need not list all 2ⁿ user sets. Both construction and evaluation have uniform polynomial bounds in the stated bit length; no approximation of budget balance, equilibrium or C(Q)≤C(P) is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute existence of an algorithm and evaluator meeting all guarantees for every promised graph, concave cost table, delay table and initial profile. A positive answer must bound bit complexity, including exact cost-share representation, and establish the equilibrium for all unilateral path deviations. Termination without a polynomial bound, a result for fixed costs alone, or an approximate equilibrium does not meet the criterion. A lower bound under a complexity assumption must state that assumption explicitly.

context_blocks.title: From an allocation to an equilibrium
context_blocks.text: The reduction receives any feasible allocation and must preserve or lower its social cost while making its output stable through budget-balanced local shares. Thus an α-approximation for the underlying allocation problem yields a protocol whose best equilibrium costs at most α times the social optimum; this is the price-of-stability connection.

context_blocks.title: The missing extension is concavity
context_blocks.text: Theorem 10 establishes polynomial time for fixed shareable costs, meaning cₑ(k) is constant for all k≥1. The following remark extends the existence and cost-preservation statements to nondecreasing discrete-concave costs but explicitly leaves polynomial time unknown. The full 2018 version repeats this as Remark 13.

context_blocks.title: The graph and strategy classes cannot be enlarged silently
context_blocks.text: The source shows that generalized series-parallel graphs can have an optimal allocation that no separable protocol enforces, even with fixed costs and no delays. Its polynomial-time result for matroid strategy sets with more general costs addresses a different family of feasible allocations.

cards.context:
The reduction receives any feasible allocation and must preserve or lower its social cost while making its output stable through budget-balanced local shares. Thus an α-approximation for the underlying allocation problem yields a protocol whose best equilibrium costs at most α times the social optimum; this is the price-of-stability connection.

Theorem 10 establishes polynomial time for fixed shareable costs, meaning cₑ(k) is constant for all k≥1. The following remark extends the existence and cost-preservation statements to nondecreasing discrete-concave costs but explicitly leaves polynomial time unknown. The full 2018 version repeats this as Remark 13.

The source shows that generalized series-parallel graphs can have an optimal allocation that no separable protocol enforces, even with fixed costs and no delays. Its polynomial-time result for matroid strategy sets with more general costs addresses a different family of feasible allocations.

The work appeared online in Mathematics of Operations Research in 2020 and in its 2021 volume. The publisher abstract still describes the connection-game result with fixed costs. This review checked that abstract and publication metadata, but could not inspect the journal’s full concave-cost remark.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
